chapter: Other bands, mutes, arrangers and composers
title: Neglected opportunities and carnival-ball rehearsals
summary: DeDroit says he turned down his uncle's rental houses and worked exhausting carnival-ball rehearsals, preferring to be a sideman.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: You'd just sit back. I'll tell you, I neglected so much but I had things so easy. My uncle, now this is aside from this, he owned a row, two rows of houses up on the river, commercial living. There was 18 Negro houses in each row. He offered it to me for nothing because he was getting tired, he was very wealthy and I refused. I didn't have time. I didn't have any sense. But I couldn't picture going around collecting for 36 Negro attendance, you know, they got about $9 a month out of the place. And I had some property of my own and I was, I don't know, I might have been big headed or something, I don't know, when I look back, the things that I neglected, I must have been happy playing music or doing something. But I was just having to try to get as much sleep as I could. I was tired all the time. I'd play a carnival ball like you know with fire but not going to have rehearsal at night at Cloud of Gale. The musicians come in, you dare not say a word to them, they're tired, they're just finished, they're tired too. So we'd go through the motions of making the rehearsal, you know. But by the time the ball came on we were fresh. But sometimes you'd have three or four rehearsals, I'd have three or four books going at the same time. And I'd put the music in myself, I had to make the cuts, you know, time it and all. I'll tell you I'm in my money. I wouldn't do that for love of money. I swear I wouldn't.
It doesn't look like it's hurt you anymore.
